hook.line: Tomás spends a whole day asking strangers the way. In Spanish, the person you ask, tell or give something to gets a small word of their own: *le*.
hook.es: ¿La señora? Le pregunté dónde queda la estación.
hook.en: The lady? I asked her where the station is.

examples.en: And Vale? I wrote to her last night.
Shall I explain the route to you? (formal)
The neighbours? I gave them my number.
What did you say to him? (to a friend)
Mariana explained the route to me.
I'll give you all the address tomorrow.

examples.es: ¿Y don Hernando? Le compré un tinto.
examples.en: And don Hernando? I bought him a coffee.

rule:
When you give, tell, ask, explain or write something to someone, Spanish names that person with a small word before the verb:
*me*: to me
*te*: to you (a friend)
*le*: to him, to her, to you (*usted*)
*nos*: to us
*les*: to them, to you all

The new ones are *le* and *les*, and they ignore gender: *le* is a man, a woman or *usted*. They are only ever for people.

English puts the person after the verb (I gave him the map). Spanish puts *le* in front: *Le di el mapa*. With *no*: *No le escribí*.

Compare *lo* and *la*: they are the person or thing itself (*lo veo*, I see him). *Le* is the one who receives (*le doy el mapa*, I give him the map). Soon you'll also hear the person named twice, *le escribí a Vale*; that's normal Spanish too.
smallPrint: Teachers call *le* and *les* indirect object pronouns.

options: I gave him the map.
I gave them the map.
He gave me the map.
I explained the route to her.
I explained the route to them.
They explained the route to me.
I wrote to her last night.
She wrote to me last night.
I wrote to her last night.
She wrote to me last night.
Can you explain the route to me? (formal)
Shall I explain the route to you? (formal)
We explained the route to him.
He explained the route to them.
He explained the route to us.
What did you say to them?
What did you say to him?
What did they say to you?
I'll give them the address.
He gives me the address.
I'll give her the address.
I'll give you my number.
Give me your number.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *le* or *les* (talking about the neighbours): ___ di mi número.
yourTurn.why: More than one person receives it, so *les*.

yourTurn.prompt: Choose *le* or *les* (talking about Vale): ___ escribí anoche.
yourTurn.why: One person, so *le*. It doesn't matter that Vale is a woman.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a stranger (*usted*): Shall I explain the route to you?
yourTurn.why: *Usted* gets *le*, the same as him or her.

yourTurn.prompt: Say: I gave him the map.
yourTurn.why: *Le* goes in front of the verb: *le di*.

yourTurn.prompt: Ask a friend: What did you say to her?
Make it plural (to them): Le di mi número.
Change who receives it to *me*: Mariana le explicó la ruta.
yourTurn.why: To me is *me*, in the same spot as *le*.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it negative: Le escribí anoche.
yourTurn.why: *No* goes in front of *le*, never between *le* and the verb.

pitfalls.why: Almost. Spanish puts *le* before the verb instead of to him after it.
The person you ask, tell or give to gets *le*, even when she's a woman.
More than one person receives it, so *les*.
*No* comes first, then *le*, then the verb.

personal: Who did you last write to, or give something to? Say it with *le* or *les*: what did you give or write, and when?
